strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis of BED formulation for LLMs, particularly the prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation pairing discussion based on complexity of state spaces
Strong empirical results with consistent improvements (2-3x over baselines) across multiple models and datasets, including robustness to model misspecification
Careful algorithmic innovations: Rao-Blackwellized EIG estimator avoiding predictive entropy fallacy, sample-then-filter approach for belief updating, hypothesis-retention mechanism
Comprehensive ablation studies including the critical data-estimation pairing alternative and important failure modes (predictive entropy insufficiency)
Clear identification and correction of flawed assumptions in prior work (Kobalczyk et al., Mazzaccara et al.) regarding EIG approximations
weaknesses: All evaluation uses LLM-based simulated answerers without human validation; unclear whether improvements transfer to realistic human interactions despite being motivated by human-facing applications

Limited task scope: only two question-answering tasks (20-Questions and movie preference elicitation); preference elicitation shows modest improvements (small effect sizes by turn 3-4); claims of 'general-purpose' approach overstated

Computational cost completely unaddressed; method appears substantially more expensive than baselines (generating N hypotheses, filtering, M candidate questions with EIG estimation) but no timing analysis or cost comparison provided

Heavy dependence on prompt engineering acknowledged but inadequately addressed; appendix notes prompts vary significantly across LLMs and exact prompting strategy 'can be quite important'; limited guidance for practitioners on transferability

Internal inconsistency in filtering justification: paper criticizes pLLM(θ; ht) for unreliability yet relies on pLLM(y; [θ, x]) for consistency checking; why trust likelihood judgments if they're inherently problematic?
LLM-as-judge evaluation for preference elicitation is somewhat circular; using LLM to score how well another LLM's recommendations match an LLM-generated persona; no external validation
Missing comparisons to relevant baselines (e.g., Handa et al. 2024 on preference elicitation, fine-tuning approaches) and no human evaluation despite applications requiring it

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis of joint model formulations (prior-likelihood vs data-estimation pairings) with clear guidance on applicability
Important correction to recent work by showing proper EIG estimation including conditional entropy substantially outperforms predictive entropy approximations
Practical innovations addressing real LLM limitations, particularly the sample-then-filter belief update strategy that addresses in-context learning failures
Strong empirical results on 20-Questions across multiple LLMs (up to 91% vs 68% baseline) with demonstrated robustness to model misspecification
Comprehensive experimental setup with multiple datasets, appropriate ablations, and careful error quantification
weaknesses: Fundamental experimental limitation: uses simulated LLM answerers rather than real humans; misspecification experiments (different LLM pairs) do not validate real-world applicability of the approach

Computational cost substantially underexplored; multiple LLM calls per question selection (15 candidates × hypothesis filtering × EIG estimation) but no runtime analysis or cost-benefit comparison to baselines

Critical design choices lack principled justification: compatibility thresholds are vague, hypothesis retention mechanism unanalyzed, decision to use uniform distribution over filtered θ is unexplained, fallback strategies appear ad-hoc

Theory-practice gap: extensive Section 4 analysis provides guidance, but practical p_f belief update significantly deviates from clean Bayesian updates without formal theoretical guarantees or convergence analysis

Active Preference Elicitation results show minimal differences between BED-LLM and Entropy baseline, questioning generality of approach; Entropy ≈ Naive QA contradicts claims about EIG importance; suggests method may be specialized to structured tasks
Statistical rigor: error bars provided but no significance tests; some differences within apparent noise levels, particularly for preference elicitation
Incremental novelty: applies well-established BED framework with careful engineering rather than algorithmic innovation; limited to multiple-choice restricted response spaces
Reproducibility concerns: method sensitive to LLM-specific choices, not all prompts in main paper, code availability not mentioned, difficult to replicate
Systematic analysis missing: no sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters (M, N, threshold), failure mode characterization, or task properties that might cause degradation
Limited scope: only two task types evaluated; comparison baselines limited (missing recent fine-tuned approaches mentioned in related work); restricted to structured information gathering scenarios

strengths: First principled application of prior-likelihood BED to LLMs that properly estimates EIG without simplifying to predictive entropy, with compelling evidence that this matters (Section 3.2.1, Figure 1)
Exceptional theoretical analysis (Section 4) providing clear guidance on when to use prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation pairings based on relative complexity of θ and y spaces
Addresses genuine practical limitations of current LLMs (poor in-context learning for user-specific variables) with the sample-then-filter mechanism
Strong empirical results on primary task: dramatic improvements across all LLMs and datasets (e.g., 14%→91% for Mistral-Large on Celebrities), with gains persisting under model misspecification
Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple LLMs tested, both same-model and cross-model scenarios, appropriate ablations (Figure 4 validates theory)
Clear, careful presentation of complex material with well-distinguished notation and extensive supporting details
weaknesses: Limited scope of task evaluation: only two task types (20-Questions and preference elicitation), with marginal improvements on the latter (~0.2-0.3 rating points), raising concerns about generalizability beyond discrete problems
No evaluation with real human users—all experiments use LLM-simulated answerers, preventing validation that improvements transfer to realistic human interaction
Computational costs not addressed: method requires sampling hypotheses, generating candidate questions, and computing EIG for each; no runtime comparisons or latency analysis provided

Several design choices are heuristic rather than principled: uniform distribution over filtered hypotheses lacks theoretical justification, filtering threshold selection is ad-hoc, and Appendix B notes LLMs 'respond differently' to diversity strategies

Missing critical ablations: no isolation of sample-then-filter contribution, no sensitivity analysis to N (hypotheses) and M (candidates), no exploration of temperature effects or filtering threshold impact
Multiple-choice restriction limits applicability to open-ended information gathering, and the paper does not explore alternative approaches for handling continuous response spaces
Limited analysis of failure modes and when simpler approaches would suffice; smaller improvements on preference elicitation suggest task-dependent effectiveness but this is not deeply investigated
Cross-model misspecification testing limited to different but similarly-capable LLMs; more extreme misspecification would strengthen claims about robustness

strengths: Clear problem motivation with relevant applications across multiple domains
Principled theoretical framework with detailed analysis of joint model formulations (Section 4) and careful justification of design choices
Technically sound approach: proper EIG formulation (Eq. 3) avoiding deterministic likelihood assumptions, Rao-Blackwellized estimator, principled belief filtering
Comprehensive experiments on 20 Questions with substantial improvements (e.g., 5.8× on Llama-3.1-8B), extensive ablations, and robustness to questioner-answerer mismatch
Practical deployment-time method applicable to any existing LLM without retraining
Thorough algorithmic specification and detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: applying well-established sequential BED framework (dating to Lindley 1956) to LLMs is somewhat incremental
Evaluation relies on synthetic settings: LLM-generated user profiles for preference elicitation and LLM answerers lacking real user behavior; no human evaluation
Weaker results on preference elicitation (modest gains ~0.3 rating points) vs. 20 Questions, raising questions about generalization
Model updating mechanism is ad-hoc: filtering threshold of 0.2 appears arbitrary with no justification or sensitivity analysis; uniform distribution assumption over filtered hypotheses is simplistic
Computational complexity underexplored: no runtime analysis, no LLM call counts provided, multiple hyperparameters (temperature, M=15, N=15, retention strategy) with limited robustness analysis

Generalization concerns: strong performance limited to 20 Questions; requires constrained output spaces (multiple-choice); conditional generation struggles with complex/overlapping hypotheses; applicability to truly open-ended information gathering unclear
Recent related work not deeply compared: Wang et al. (2025), Chan et al. (2025), Kobalczyk et al. (2025) mentioned but comparisons limited to Naive and Split baselines
Theoretical justification gaps: Section 4 analysis is largely intuitive rather than formally rigorous; no convergence or approximation quality analysis

strengths: Clear problem motivation and principled information-theoretic approach using established BED framework
Thoughtful design justification, especially the prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation analysis in Section 4
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models and domains with substantial ablations
Strong empirical improvements on 20 Questions (e.g., 5.8× for Llama-3.1-8B)
Extensive appendices with detailed algorithmic exposition and justifications
Demonstrates robustness to questioner-answerer model mismatch
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: applies established BED and Rao-Blackwellized estimation to LLMs; filtering-based belief update is straightforward rejection sampling
Evaluation relies heavily on artificial LLM-as-answerer setup with explicit ground truth; no human evaluation despite motivating real-world applications (medical diagnosis, preference learning)
Computational cost not addressed: requires ~1200+ LLM forward passes per turn with no runtime analysis or efficiency comparison
Weak baseline comparisons: 'Split' is somewhat strawmanned; missing comparisons to recent active learning and uncertainty quantification methods
Problem selection bias: favorable 20 Questions domain; preference elicitation shows modest gains (0.2-0.3 rating), suggesting limited generalizability to open-ended tasks
Hyperparameter sensitivity not explored: filtering threshold, temperature, diversity parameters vary across experiments without ablation
Theoretical gaps: alignment argument (Section B.3) is informal; no convergence analysis or guarantees on EIG estimation error
Insufficient mechanistic analysis: minimal explanation of when/why the method works, what hypotheses are maintained, or qualitative examples of selected questions

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addresses genuine limitation of LLMs in multi-turn adaptive questioning with broad applications (preference learning, clarification, debugging, medical diagnosis)

Principled and careful approach: Thoughtful treatment of core design decisions including prior-likelihood vs. data-estimation pairing (Section 4), rejection of deterministic likelihood assumptions, and filtering-based belief updating strategy

Strong experimental validation: 5.8× improvement on 20 Questions with small models (Llama-3.1-8B), consistent 2× improvements across most settings, comprehensive ablations across 5 model sizes/families (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B), robustness to questioner-answerer mismatch

Technically sound: Correct EIG formulation with Rao-Blackwellized variance reduction, well-designed ablations isolating each component's contribution, proper statistical reporting with standard errors

Excellent presentation: Clear narrative with well-structured sections, particularly strong treatment of design choices in Section 4, informative figures demonstrating when/why EIG differs from entropy, comprehensive appendix with implementation details and prompts

Practical applicability: Works with frozen LLMs at deployment time without retraining, applicable to any existing LLM, demonstrates broad applicability across discrete and continuous-valued target spaces
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: Only 2 main experimental domains (20 Questions, preference elicitation) despite mentioning numerous applications (medical diagnosis, IT automation, troubleshooting, tutoring); preference elicitation improvements are modest (~0.2-0.3 rating points out of 5), raising questions about applicability to less-structured domains

Missing computational cost analysis: No quantification of computational overhead per turn (LLM calls for candidate generation, EIG computation for M candidates, N hypothesis samples, filtering); unclear how cost compares to simpler baselines, critical for adoption decisions

Belief updating strategy involves multiple design choices of limited generality: Compatibility threshold (0.2), temperature hyperparameter varies by task (1.3 for 20Q, 1.0 for preferences), number of filtering iterations (2-3); limited sensitivity analysis or principled selection mechanism

Hypothesis space complexity and generality unclear: Method tested on semantically coherent spaces (20 Questions) and structured text descriptions (preferences); unclear performance on truly unstructured, high-dimensional continuous, or adversarially biased hypothesis spaces

Entropy ablation performs surprisingly well in several cases: On Llama-3.1-8B for Animals achieves 54±5.0 vs. BED-LLM's 63±4.9; inconsistent gaps across models suggest full EIG may not always be necessary, but this not thoroughly explored

Limited baseline diversity: Compared mainly to Naive and Split baselines (latter acknowledged as flawed); no comparison to established active learning strategies or uncertainty-based baselines from related work despite mentioning multiple prior approaches

Model misspecification evaluation limited: Only tested with questioner-answerer from different LLM families; unclear behavior with fundamentally biased, adversarial, or noisy response distributions beyond model family mismatch

Likelihood remains fixed: Assumes p(y|θ) need not update because beliefs on θ capture all information; may not hold in complex settings where responses depend on context history, no empirical validation provided
